content:
If I could change one thing about iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, it would be disabling that new downward-swipe gesture that summons Siri AI. There are already plenty of existing ways to launch Siri, and this new action won't affect my habit of pulling down on iPhone and iPad to open the Notification Center.

As for the Mac, macOS 27 Golden Gate is almost entirely good news. Even at the end of August, new betas are still adding welcome changes. However, before macOS 27 officially launches next month, there is still one change I would like to see.

macOS 27 Golden Gate makes MacBook battery percentage harder to read

macOS 27 Golden Gate has redesigned the battery control item in the menu bar. By default, it doesn't show the percentage—just a battery-shaped icon.

In this state, it looks fine. I've also disabled the percentage readout on my iPhone, which uses a similar battery icon. However, I've always liked checking the percentage on my Mac.

If you turn on the 'Show Percentage' option in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the number is placed inside the battery icon. I'm guessing this is to keep the design consistent with the iPhone in iOS 27.

Putting the percentage inside the battery icon on iPhone was a workaround Apple adopted to address the cramped space to the right of the notch or Dynamic Island. But on the Mac, even in the menu bar, I don't have that lack of screen space issue.

I've been running macOS 27 Golden Gate on a 15-inch MacBook Air since the first developer beta. I find myself paying less attention to the battery percentage overall, because it's harder for my eyes to read.

I hope Apple will reconsider this design decision going forward, especially if it bothers more users. In the meantime, I've at least solved the problem for myself.

I used Codex to build a simple menu bar utility that clearly displays the current battery status and percentage the way I want. If you find it useful too, you can download and install it for free here.
